standard.title: Evaluate with design criteria
standard.description: use given or co-developed design criteria including sustainability to evaluate design ideas and solutions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can evaluate the success of design ideas and solutions based on personal preferences and including sustainability (AC9TDE2P03). They have evaluated based on personal judgement. They have not yet used explicit design criteria as the basis for evaluation or co-developed criteria with others.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use given or co-developed design criteria — including sustainability — to evaluate design ideas and solutions, with reasons grounded in the criteria.

nodes.label: Understanding design criteria as evaluation tools
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what design criteria are and describe what a solution would need to do to meet a given criterion
nodes.minimum_width: Read a set of given design criteria and explain in plain language what a solution must do to satisfy at least two of them
nodes.typical_width: Read and interpret design criteria for different design problems; explain what each criterion requires of a solution; distinguish between criteria that are met and criteria that are not met for a given solution
wider: Examine design criteria that include universal design principles (flexible use, low physical effort, intuitive use) — explain what each principle means as a design requirement and how it addresses social sustainability
Compare two sets of criteria for the same problem — discuss how different criteria lead to different design priorities and potentially different solutions
success_criteria: Explains what at least two criteria require of a solution
Distinguishes between criteria and solution (criteria state what the solution must do; they are not the solution itself)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot interpret what a criterion requires of a solution cannot co-develop meaningful criteria in N2 or evaluate against them in N3 — the evaluation task requires correctly reading the criteria first.

nodes.label: Co-developing design criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can contribute to developing design criteria with others, including at least one criterion related to sustainability
nodes.minimum_width: Contribute at least one criterion to a co-developed set, explaining why it matters for the design problem
nodes.typical_width: Co-develop design criteria with others for a design problem; include criteria addressing function, safety, sustainability and user needs; explain the reasoning behind each criterion
wider: Develop design criteria that include a social sustainability criterion addressing accessibility for different user groups — explain how this criterion reflects universal design thinking

Develop criteria for a product that will be evaluated by users from different cultural backgrounds — discuss how criteria might need to reflect diverse needs and what this reveals about how criteria are never fully neutral

response_modes.reason: Students who only develop criteria for one type of problem (e.g. a toy) may not see that criteria development is always contextual. Developing criteria across different problem types and user groups builds the habit of thinking from the user's perspective rather than the designer's preferences.

success_criteria: Contributes at least one criterion with a stated reason
The contributed criterion addresses something a solution must do, not a preference

nodes.label: Evaluating ideas and solutions against criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate a design idea or solution against criteria — including sustainability — and provide reasons grounded in the criteria
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate one design idea or solution against at least two criteria and state whether each criterion is met, with a reason for each judgement
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate design ideas and solutions against criteria including sustainability across different design contexts; use evaluation to revise and select between design ideas; reflect on how well the final solution meets the criteria
wider: Compare the waste produced by different design ideas and the potential for recycling — use sustainability criteria to evaluate and select between design ideas based on material choices

Evaluate a designed solution against criteria that include safety, sustainability and community/cultural appropriateness — discuss cases where criteria compete (e.g. a more sustainable material is less durable) and how to reason through trade-offs

response_modes.reason: Evaluating against criteria requires criterion-by-criterion reasoning, not an overall impression. Scaffolding the process prevents students from simply stating a preference. The reasoning move (identify criterion → check solution → state match/gap → give reason) needs to become habitual.

Evaluation integrates criteria knowledge (node 1), co-developed criteria (node 2), and knowledge of materials and sustainability (AC9TDE4K01, K02) into a practical judgement. The coordination of multiple knowledge sources in an evaluation task is the descriptor's full demand.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The sustainability evaluation direction — comparing material waste, recyclability and durability across design ideas — is genuinely rich and directly connects to the descriptor's inclusion of sustainability as a criterion type. Students can engage with real trade-offs that go well beyond 'does it meet the criteria?'
success_criteria: States whether each criterion is met with a reason
At least one criterion involves sustainability
Evaluation references the solution's features, not just personal preference
